Hi I'm Carmel Crimmins in London. It's Thursday September 10th today. Will AI kill us all. A warning from inside the tech industry. Trump offers Americans a five thousand dollar payout if Republicans win the midterms. Apple drops its two thousand dollar foldable iPhone and Iran gets its hands on U.S. military tech. This is Reuters World News, bringing you everything you need to know from the front lines in ten minutes, seven days a week. We start with a bombshell warning from inside the AI industry. Researchers at AI giant Anthropic are warning that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity within the decade, with one resigning over it, saying the companies building this tech are gambling with our lives. Mike Dolan from our sister podcast Morning Bid has more.
Will AI kill us all? I don't think anybody in financial markets can price the end of humanity, but what these apocalyptic warnings do point to, and I think we have seen many this year, including in the spring, about mass depression and mass unemployment, and again, subsequently, about the wipeout of entire financial sectors. Warnings recur but they point overwhelmingly to regulation of this new technology and this is the real impact that can potentially be priced, although in this geopolitical climate it's hard to imagine any joined up thinking on regulation of something that is a global transformation.
I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.
U.S. President Donald Trump making an extraordinary pitch at the Republicans' first ever midterm convention in Dallas. A $5,000 Trump dividend if the Republicans keep control of Congress in November's midterm elections.
Very much like a successful company will do a cash distribution to a shareholder.
It's not clear how any such payout would work, or if it's even legal. With approximately 270 million US adults, the idea would cost over $1 trillion. Republicans are hoping the convention will energize voters ahead of November. Democratic Senator John Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with his party, made a surprise video appearance at the event. With polls showing Democrats more motivated to vote, Republicans are banking on Trump to energize their base, despite voter anxiety about inflation and the Iran war. But the strategy has its skeptics. Many Republicans in competitive races skipping the event worry that Trump's brand may not be enough. Reporter Nandita Bose is in Dallas.
It has been really interesting speaking to folks here. A lot of people are concerned about you know high gas prices. They are concerned about the cost of living. But somehow they do not wish to tie that to President Trump. When they speak about their economic anxieties, they are not taking that back to the president. And they want the war to end. They're bringing up Iran in conversations and how that has impacted the cost of goods and groceries and, first, you know, energy prices. But somehow they're not taking that back to the President of the United States. So we'll see, you know, we're gonna do more interviews and talk to people to see, who is it really they think is responsible for the war and for energy prices. But people here are really not tying a lot of what we're seeing in terms of economic concerns to the president.
Now the president's journey to Dallas didn't go exactly to plan. An emergency slide on Air Force One accidentally deployed before he boarded, briefly delaying his departure. He flew on the Boeing 747 gifted by Qatar, telling reporters he was confident the plane was safe or he wouldn't have used it. Now the convention was definitely not the biggest event on prime time TV last night. That honor went to the NFL, where the Seahawks beat the New England Patriots in season's first matchup. Tough competition for the Republicans. But perhaps the buzziest event of the day belonged to Apple, the iPhone maker revealing its latest phone, and it folds. The Duo, its first ever foldable phone, is a passport-sized device that will retail for $1,999. The launch marks the biggest overhaul of the iPhone since 2007, and is a big deal for new CEO John Ternus. Reporter Stephen Nellis was there and got to play around with it.
This is going to take Apple to a brand new category, that's mostly been dominated by Android devices from Samsung, Huawei, and others. It's going to cost $2,000 to start and will have the biggest screen and most advanced chip of any iPhone. So Apple's done a lot of work to try to fix some things that have bedeviled other folding phones in the past. Number one is this hinge. It has to feel smoothly secure, hundreds of times a day sometimes, and thousands if not millions of times over the lifetime of the device. Number two is looking at the screen and seeing whether you can see any kind of a crease. Apple deployed some amazing technology from the chip-making industry to try to minimize what you see there in terms of a crease.
Stephen says it's also a new showcase for Apple's artificial intelligence offerings.
This thing is really optimized for the new Siri that Apple brought out in the summertime that is hoping users in the US will adopt. There's still some key question marks though. The new Siri will not be available in the EU and it's not gonna be available in China leaving a lot of people wondering how Apple is going to introduce the most important new features and its most important advice in a timely way by the end of this week.
To Iran now, where Tehran's capture of a US underwater drone near the Strait of Hormuz this week highlights the way in which warfare is changing. The US military is increasingly relying on new autonomous technology. The Pentagon says the 19-foot submersible malfunctioned and was an older model carrying non-sensitive data, while Iran is touting the seizure as a capture of advanced US technology. And analysts say Tehraan is likely to reverse-engineer it. Our Pentagon reporter Idrees Ali explains.
This U.S. military submarine made by Anduril, the private company, is capable of surveying the seabed, carrying out countermine missions. It's about 20 feet long, essentially, and it can be active and working for 10 days or so without needing to return to base or charge. I think it speaks to the fact that drones as a whole are a focal point of warfare around the world. We've seen it in places like Ukraine and Russia. And now we're seeing countries like the United States and other ones really focusing and relying on them because at the end of the day, if you're a country, you do not want your sailors or soldiers being put in harm's way. And the best way to do that is drones. I do think it is important to note that early in the conflict, we did see the US military release footage of another underwater drone actually being used to target Iranian ships in some of their ports. So they have played more of a role in this conflict than in previous ones, and I think the expectation is that that's only going to proliferate.
The Trump administration is proposing changing the census to count only U.S. citizens and permanent residents. It's a move that could dramatically shift political representation and federal funding across the country. The proposal would exclude not just immigrants in the U.S. illegally, but also those in the country legally on a temporary basis, and would eliminate some of the questions about race and ethnicity that have been part of the census since 1790. Civil rights advocates warn the changes could leave cities and states with large immigrant populations with insufficient federal aid and representation, calling the potential effects earth-shattering. New financial disclosures released by the White House reveal that President Trump gave cash gifts of up to $45,000 to close aides last year, including executive assistant Natalie Harp and three others working in the West Wing. The payments, equivalent to roughly one-third of the aid's government salaries are raising ethics concerns since federal employees are generally barred from receiving compensation beyond their official pay. The White House says the gifts comply with ethics rules and are part of Trump's long-standing practice of giving Christmas gifts. History fans are flocking to London's British Museum today to catch a rare glimpse of 11th century life in the Bayeux Tapestry. That's a 70-meter-long embroidery depicting the Norman conquest of England. Producer Mary-Louise Gumuchian got a sneak peek at the thousand-year-old artwork before the exhibit's opening.
It's normally housed in a museum in France, but it arrived on loan in July in an air-conditioned anti-vibration crate escorted by French police until the Euro tunnel and then handed over to British authorities once it arrived in Britain. Such is the excitement for this exhibition that tickets for a first phase sold out within hours.
